newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-N.Petroleum wants to spread wings.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-N.Petroleum wants to spread wings.

text.p: Northern Petroleum Plc, the junior oil firm active in Russia's Arctic, is keen to move on to other countries and bigger things.
The company wants to widen its horizon as it is about to take a new, big shareholder on board, chief executive Peter Clutterbuck said.
"We are quite anxious to diversify out of Russia and to add in additional non-Russian assets," he told Reuters.
"We are confident about Russia, but the markets are nervous about the country and they would prefer us to have a non-Russian element in our portfolio," he said in a recent interview.
Northern wants to expand with the financial backing of the Malaysian Mining Corporation Bhd, which agreed in January in principle to take a stake of about 46 percent in Northern.
"The bigger projects which we could not possibly access on our own, we would enter with MMC," said Clutterbuck.
MMC is currently conducting a due diligence investigation and details on how and when it will take a stake in Northern have yet to be worked out.
Clutterbuck said MMC, which is branching out into the gas and oil industry, may take up its planned 46 percent interest in one go or in tranches.
The contact with MMC was established through Australia's Cityview NL, in which the Malaysian company took a 45.6 percent stake late in 1996.
Northern Petroleum's board member Mark Smyth is also on the board of Cityview, which will focus on oil projects in South East Asia.
In contrast, Northern is looking for new projects in Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries as well as the Middle East.
"MMC's strategy is to focus very much on islamic countries," said Clutterbuck, adding Northern was already looking at a large number of deals outside the former Soviet Union.

Clutterbuck said no eventual takeover by MMC was in the pipeline. Instead, Northern aims for a full listing on the London Stock Exchange after it was floated on the Alternative Investment Market (AIM) in 1995.
"They (MMC) will have a high degree of control. It will allow Northern to upgrade from an AIM listing to a full listing," Clutterbuck said.
The main asset of Northern Petroleum, which was founded in 1994, is its 10.3 percent interest in Russian joint stock company Polar Bear, which has three oil fields in north west Russia.
The main field is Tedin which was discovered in 1989. It has estimated recoverable proven and probable reserves of 85 million barrels of oil and is expected to come onstream mid-1998.
The field is located north of the Arctic circle, in the Timan-Pechora region where other western companies such as Conoco, Exxon, Texaco, BHP and BG are also active.
Conoco's Polar Lights venture already began production in 1994 and saw output rise over 50 percent in 1996 to 37,500 barrels per day (bpd).
Tedin's production is expected to be 35,000 bpd.
Northern, which has the right to raise its interest in Polar Bear to 35 percent, is the only junior firm with interests the area.
Clutterbuck is open to participation of a major oil firm in Polar Bear, although he is wary because it might well lead to higher costs for the whole venture.
Oil majors usually have to stick to high western standards, while Northern takes a more relaxed stance, allowing it to operate more cheaply than many of its rivals, Clutterbuck said.
"For example, if the environmental standards would be met within the Russian legislation that would be good enough for us," he said.
